reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Axial Load Transfer
sections.body: Drilled shafts transmit axial compression and uplift loads through side resistance Rs and base (tip) resistance RB. Load transfer mechanics (Kulhawy 1991, O'Neill and Reese 1972): Side resistance mobilized first at small displacements (~1/2 inch for full mobilization); base resistance mobilizes at larger displacements (~4-5% of diameter B for cohesive soil and rock; ~10% B for cohesionless soils). Three components: side resistance Rs, base resistance RB, and combined total resistance QT. Between peak side and peak base resistance, side resistance may increase or decrease depending on stress-strain behavior at shaft-soil interface (softening possible in some materials). Design for service limit states must account for differences in mobilization displacement for side vs. base resistance.
key_points: Side resistance mobilizes at ~1/2 inch displacement; base resistance at ~4-10% of shaft diameter
Displacement for maximum base resistance: 4-5% B (cohesive/rock) or 10% B (cohesionless)
Side resistance mobilizes first; peak side and peak base occur at different displacements
Service limit state design must account for differences in side vs. base mobilization

sections.applicability: Axial design of all drilled shafts; basis for step-by-step design procedure

sections.title: Relationship to Overall Design Process
sections.body: Chapter constitutes detailed treatment of Block 11 ('Establish Minimum Depth and Diameter for Axial Loads') of the overall design process (Figure 8-1, Chapter 8). AASHTO (2017a) identifies axial compression and uplift of single drilled shafts as strength limit states; settlement control as service limit state. Factored axial force effects communicated by structural engineer to foundation designer for each applicable limit state and scour condition. For cohesive soils in Service I load combination, transient loads can be omitted from settlement analysis.
key_points: Block 11 of overall design process: minimum depth and diameter for axial loads
Strength limit states: axial compression and uplift
Service limit state: settlement control
Transient loads may be omitted from settlement analysis in cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Relates axial design to overall design process; limit state identification

sections.title: Step-by-Step Procedure: Design for Axial Load
sections.body: 7-step LRFD design procedure: (1) Idealize subsurface profile — divide into geomaterial layers; classify each as cohesionless (GW, GP, GM, SW, SP, SM, ML), cohesive (GC, SC, CL, CH, MH), or rock. Scour conditions must be reflected in profiles. (2) Establish limit states and factored axial loads — review applicable limit states and load combinations per Chapter 8. (3) Assign geomaterial properties — cohesionless soils: SPT N60 and (N1)60, effective stress friction angle φ', σ'v; cohesive soils: undrained shear strength su; rock: uniaxial compressive strength qu, RQD, GSI. Use mean values for LRFD; COV limits: N-values ≤45%, su ≤35%. (4) Select trial lengths and diameters — L/B typically 3-30; soil depths to 100 ft and diameters to 8 ft are routine; depths to 200 ft and diameters to 12 ft are within range of well-equipped specialty contractors; rock sockets up to 50 ft possible; in-soil overburden diameter ≥6 in. larger than rock socket to allow rock drilling tools to pass. (5) Compute nominal unit side and base resistances (Step 5 — detailed design methods per Section 10.3.5). (6) Satisfy strength limit states — check ΣηiγiFi ≤ ΣφiRi; resistance factors φ per AASHTO and agency experience; iterate on length and diameter as needed. (7) Satisfy service limit states — conduct load-deformation analysis; mobilized side and base resistance at axial displacement corresponding to tolerable deformation.
key_points: 7-step procedure matching Block 11 of overall design process
Geomaterial classification: cohesionless, cohesive, or rock for each layer
Routine: soil to 100 ft depth, diameter to 8 ft; specialty: to 200 ft, to 12 ft diameter
In-soil overburden diameter ≥6 in. larger than rock socket for tool passage
COV limits: N-values ≤45%; su ≤35% for applying tabulated resistance factors
LRFD: ΣηiγiFi ≤ ΣφiRi for each applicable strength limit state
equations: Eq. 10-1: ΣηiγiFi ≤ ΣφiRi — LRFD check for strength limit states

sections.title: Calculate Nominal Side and Base Resistances (Step 5)
sections.body: Cohesionless soils — side resistance: Beta method (effective stress): fs = βσ'v; β = K tan δ; for SPT: β = 1.5 - 0.245z^0.5 (Rollins et al. 2005) for N60 ≥ 15; limits: β ≤ 1.8 for z ≤ 5 m, β ≤ 1.2 for z > 5 m; for CPT: direct method. Cohesionless soils — base resistance: qb = Nq*σ'v (AASHTO O'Neill & Reese 1999 method); Nq based on SPT N-value; CPT-based methods also available. Cohesive soils — side resistance: Alpha (total stress) method: fs = α*su; α from O'Neill and Reese (1999): α = 0.55 for su/pa ≤ 1.5; α = 0.55 - 0.1(su/pa - 1.5) for 1.5 ≤ su/pa ≤ 2.5; FSU method from Reese and O'Neill (1988). Cohesive soils — base resistance: qb = Ncp*su; Ncp = 9 for L/B ≥ 3 (AASHTO); reduction for lower L/B. Rock — side resistance: fs = τmax based on socket diameter, rock type, and qu; Carter & Kulhawy (1988) normalized method; Horvath & Kenney (1979) for soft rock; Rowe & Armitage (1987) for rough sockets. Rock — base resistance: qb = 3qu for L/B > 0.5 (AASHTO); or qb = Ksp*qu using Rowe & Armitage bearing capacity factor. RESISTANCE FACTORS (AASHTO 2017): side resistance — with load test: 0.65 (O'Neill and Reese method); without load test: 0.45; base resistance — with load test: 0.50; without load test: 0.40; uplift side resistance — with load test: 0.60; without load test: 0.40.
key_points: Cohesionless side: Beta method fs = βσ'v; β = 1.5 - 0.245z^0.5 for N60 ≥ 15
Cohesive side: Alpha method fs = αsu; α = 0.55 for su/pa ≤ 1.5
Cohesive base: qb = 9su for L/B ≥ 3
Rock side: Carter & Kulhawy (1988) normalized method; rough sockets increase resistance
Rock base: qb = 3qu for L/B > 0.5 (AASHTO); or Ksp*qu per Rowe & Armitage
Resistance factors: φside = 0.65 (with load test) / 0.45 (without); φbase = 0.50 (with) / 0.40 (without)
equations: Beta method: fs = βσ'v; β = 1.5 - 0.245z^0.5 (Rollins 2005) for cohesionless side resistance
Alpha method: fs = αsu; α = 0.55 (su/pa ≤ 1.5), α = 0.55 - 0.1(su/pa - 1.5) (1.5 ≤ su/pa ≤ 2.5)
Cohesive base: qb = Ncp*su; Ncp = 9 for L/B ≥ 3
sections.applicability: Computation of nominal side and base resistance for all geomaterial types

sections.title: Design for Uplift
sections.body: Uplift capacity: side resistance only (base resistance = 0 for uplift). Nominal uplift resistance Rup = sum of nominal unit side resistances over shaft length (same methods as compression). AASHTO resistance factor for uplift side resistance with load test: φup = 0.60; without load test: φup = 0.40. Service limit state for uplift: control of axial deflection (extension under uplift) and progressive debonding of concrete from soil. Design check: factored uplift demand ≤ φup*Rup. For combined uplift and moment, interaction between side resistance and flexural demands must be checked.
key_points: Uplift capacity: side resistance only; base resistance = 0
Resistance factors: φup = 0.60 with load test; 0.40 without
Service limit: control axial extension; check progressive debonding
sections.applicability: Design of drilled shafts subjected to net uplift forces

sections.title: Design for Scour
sections.body: Scour reduces effective shaft length contributing to axial resistance. Design flood scour (Strength I): remove side and base resistance from scoured zone; check adequate resistance remains; also re-check lateral load resistance with reduced embedment. Scour check flood (Extreme Event II): more severe scour; check shaft tip depth provides adequate resistance. Three types of scour: general scour (entire channel cross-section), contraction scour (narrowing of flow area), local scour (around piers). Degradation scour (long-term channel bed lowering) must also be assessed. Side resistance above final scour elevation NOT counted. AASHTO: γEQ = 0.5 for Extreme Event II. Where scour controls, shaft must be extended deeper into the non-scoured stratum.
key_points: Scour: remove side and base resistance from scoured zone for all limit states
Design flood scour: Strength I; Check flood scour: Extreme Event II
Degradation scour (long-term) must be assessed in addition to design and check flood scour
Side resistance above final scour elevation not counted
sections.applicability: Drilled shaft design in stream environments subject to scour

sections.title: Downdrag
sections.body: Downdrag occurs when soil settles relative to shaft, reversing side resistance direction from upward (positive) to downward (negative). Common causes: consolidation of soft soils under fill or surcharge; liquefaction-induced ground settlement; drainage of soft soils. AASHTO: downdrag is a load effect (DD, factored by γDD = 1.25 for Strength I and IV); added to structural load demands. Shaft length must be sufficient that resistance below neutral plane (where side resistance reverses) equals sum of factored structural loads plus factored downdrag. Strategies to reduce downdrag: bituminous coating on shaft (reduces side adhesion in settling stratum); preloading or surcharging fill before construction; slender shafts in settling zone; use of pile isolation collar. Post-liquefaction downdrag: shaft settles with liquefied zone; combined kinematic + downdrag loading; compute using residual strength of liquefied soils.
key_points: Downdrag: soil settles relative to shaft; reverses side resistance to downward force
AASHTO: downdrag is load DD; γDD = 1.25 for Strength I and IV
Neutral plane: depth where cumulative side resistance equals structural + downdrag loads
Mitigation: bituminous coating; preloading; slender shafts in settling zone
Post-liquefaction downdrag: kinematic + downdrag; use residual strength of liquefied soils
sections.applicability: Drilled shafts in settling soils; fills over soft ground; post-liquefaction conditions

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter presented step-by-step LRFD procedure for design of drilled shafts under axial loading. Three geomaterial types (cohesionless, cohesive, rock) each with appropriate side and base resistance methods. Resistance factors depend on whether load testing is included in the project. Special considerations include scour, downdrag, and seismic effects on axial resistance. Design methods consistent with AASHTO LRFD 2017a.
